page: Amazon Web Services c5.24xlarge is a compute-optimized server instance built on the AWS Nitro hypervisor. The system is driven by a 96-vCPU Intel Xeon 8275CL processor configured with 48 physical cores and two threads per core, operating at a base frequency of 3.6 GHz on the x86_64 architecture. Hardware features include 35 MB of L3 cache, along with support for AVX, AVX-512F, and AVX-512 VNNI vector instruction sets. Memory capacity totals 192.0 GB of DDR4 RAM clocked at 3 GHz, establishing a compute-oriented allocation ratio of 2.0 GB per vCPU. The instance does not include integrated local storage or GPU accelerators, while providing a 25 Gbps baseline network throughput.

Benchmark results demonstrate strong multi-threaded computational capacity. Multi-core evaluations—including stress-ng multi-core (94,532.05), PassMark CPU (62,868.74), and Clang software compilation (42,224.0)—place the instance within the top quartile of tested systems. High memory throughput supports these compute metrics, reaching 232.37 GB/sec on large-block uncached reads and handling 79.45 million Redis SET operations per second. In contrast, single-thread metrics fall within median bands, as seen in stress-ng single-core (1,566.7) and Geekbench single-core (1,400.0) scores. Tasks involving autoregressive LLM text generation perform poorly due to the lack of hardware accelerators.

From a resource utilization standpoint, the instance offers strong compute density for organizations needing high core counts without the cost overhead of dedicated local NVMe arrays or GPU hardware. Relying exclusively on network-attached storage requires workloads to tolerate remote disk I/O characteristics, but it maximizes flexibility for stateless processing architectures.

Amazon Web Services c5.24xlarge is targeted at compute-heavy, highly parallel workloads. Appropriate deployments include distributed continuous integration and compilation pipelines, CPU-based ray tracing, scientific batch simulations, high-traffic web backends, and in-memory key-value processing clusters.
